title: Vaccine Hesitancy and Exposure to Misinformation: a Survey Analysis
screen_reason: Web survey of 600 Florida adults (June 2021) that asked whether respondents had read or heard each of eight named COVID-19 vaccine misinformation claims in the previous 6 months, and reports that 73.2% encountered at least one. That is a share of survey respondents who say they were exposed to misinformation - a RECALL (self-reported exposure) estimate with a stated denominator.

estimates.platform: web-based survey; respondents were asked whether they had 'read or heard' the claims, with no platform or channel specified
estimates.date: Fielded 3-14 June 2021; the exposure question covers 'the past 6 months', i.e. roughly December 2020 to June 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of adults who report having read or heard at least one of eight named COVID-19 vaccine misinformation claims in the past 6 months
estimates.value_raw: 73.2% ('nearly three-quarters of respondents (73.2%)'); the abstract rounds this to 73%. Table 3 gives the complement verbatim: 'Did not report any misinformation exposure 161, 26.8' of n = 600
estimates.denominator: 600 adults aged 18 and over resident in Florida, USA; stratified quota sample purchased from the market-research panel Prodege MR, with quotas by region of the state for gender, age, race, education and ethnicity; stated margin of error +/- 4 points at 95% confidence
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to having read or heard at least one of eight specific misinformation claims about COVID-19 vaccines in the previous 6 months. The eight: vaccines contain a 'live strain' of the virus; vaccines contain 5G microchips; vaccination will be mandated by the CDC; vaccines modify people's genes and alter their DNA; vaccines may cause infertility; vaccines were designed to reduce the world's population; the virus was created before the pandemic in order to increase vaccine sales; the daughter of the Russian president died from the vaccine.
estimates.misinfo_def: No abstract definition is given; misinformation is operationalised as eight named claims chosen from an academic literature review and current public health guidance - "A majority of these themes have been identified by the CDC as being among the most critical falsehoods effecting vaccine hesitancy" - and deliberately mixing "medical misinformation as well as some political/conspiratorial misinformation themes".
estimates.source_quote: According to the survey results, exposure to misinformation has been widespread, with nearly three-quarters of respondents (73.2%) reporting some degree of misinformation exposure in the referenced time period.
estimates.page_loc: Findings, 'Misinformation Exposure and Vaccination', p. 182; Table 3, p. 183; also Abstract, p. 179
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The EXPOSURE event is self-reported: respondents said whether they had read or heard each claim, with no verification and no time-ordering. The FALSITY of the claims, however, was fixed in advance by the researchers from an academic literature review and public-health guidance (largely the CDC's 'Myths and facts about COVID-19 vaccines'), so unlike a generic 'have you seen misinformation?' item this instrument names eight independently established falsehoods - a materially stronger recall design. Multiple quality-control items were embedded and failures excluded; a principal-components factor analysis (varimax, n = 600) found no distinct medical vs political factors, so the eight items are treated as one exposure count. No reliability coefficient is reported for the eight-item battery.
estimates.moderator_quote: In order to measure exposure to vaccine-related misinformation, we asked respondents whether they encountered each of eight common misinformation themes in the previous 6 months. Misinformation themes were identified based on an academic literature review, as well as current public health guidance. ... Sample for the survey was purchased through an industry-leading market research provider (Prodege MR), and survey respondents were selected using a stratified, quota sampling approach to ensure representativeness.
estimates.notes: Arithmetic checks: 100 - 26.8 = 73.2 and 600 - 161 = 439 (73.17%), so the printed 73.2% and Table 3's 161/26.8 are consistent; the abstract's '73%' is the same number rounded. THREE THINGS AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD SEE. (1) CLOSED-LIST DESIGN: this is exposure to eight PRE-SPECIFIED claims, not to misinformation in general, so it is a floor for any-exposure - the authors say so ('it is likely that information consumers encounter a host of additional misinformation') - while at the same time the list was deliberately stocked with the most salient CDC-flagged falsehoods, which pushes it up relative to a random claim set. It is not comparable to open-ended 'have you come across false information?' items. (2) One of the eight items, 'COVID-19 vaccines will be mandated by the CDC' (36.3%), is a prediction about future policy rather than a verifiably false statement of fact, and it contributes to the 73.2%; the other seven are unambiguous falsehoods. (3) Geography is SUBNATIONAL: Florida only, not the United States as a whole, and the authors themselves call for national replication. country_norm is United States because that is the canonical country name, but the row should not be read as a US national estimate. QUOTE NOTE: quote_verbatim = false. The sentence is copied exactly as printed in the article, but the text file interleaves the two page columns line by line (Table 2 runs down the left column while this sentence runs down the right) and also breaks 'respon-dents' across a line, so no contiguous span of the text file reproduces it. The only contiguous fragment carrying the value is the single line 'dents (73.2%) reporting some degree of misinformation expo-'. The complement is independently verifiable in Table 3: 'Did not report any misinformation exposure 161 26.8'.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and NOT extracted. (1) THE EIGHT PER-CLAIM EXPOSURE RATES, Table 3, all verbatim with counts out of 600: 'live strain' of the virus 257 (42.8%); 5G microchips 231 (38.5%); will be mandated by the CDC 218 (36.3%); modify genes / alter DNA 218 (36.3%); may cause infertility 207 (34.5%); designed to reduce the world's population 182 (30.3%); created before the pandemic to increase vaccine sales 113 (18.8%); daughter of the Russian president died from the vaccine 36 (6.0%). These were left as one aggregate row rather than eight, because the paper treats the eight items as one battery ('providing a strong proxy measure for overall misinformation exposure') and a factor analysis found no distinct sub-dimensions, and because eight rows from a single 600-person survey would over-weight this study. If the review codes claim-level exposure, these eight are ready to add as definition_variant rows against the same denominator. (2) Vaccination outcomes, which are not misinformation shares: 64.3% had at least one dose, 57.8% fully vaccinated, and all of Table 2's demographic and partisan breakdowns (Democrats 73.4%, Republicans 58.5%, Independents 56.5%; 65+ 84.0% vs 18-24 42.6%). (3) Tables 4 and 5, vaccination rate BY exposure (73.8% among the unexposed down to 52.2% at six or more themes; per-theme vaccinated/not-vaccinated splits) - these are the study's dose-response finding, an association between exposure and behaviour, not a prevalence of exposure. (4) Objections to vaccination among the 97 who said they probably/definitely would not vaccinate (side effects 74.2%, created too quickly 50.5%, not effective 20.6%, etc.) - beliefs and attitudes, explicitly outside the review's scope. (5) 45.3% of the 214 not-yet-vaccinated saying they probably/definitely would not vaccinate; 32.3% having discussed vaccination with their primary care provider; the logit odds ratios in Table 6. (6) Externally cited figures that R8 forbids keeping: 48.6% of eligible Americans fully vaccinated (CDC, June 2021), Florida accounting for 17.4% of new US infections, and the 6.4 / 6.2 percentage-point declines in vaccination intent from Loomba et al.

rob.design: Cross-sectional web-based survey of 600 adults aged 18+ in Florida, USA, fielded 3-14 June 2021. Sample purchased from Prodege MR, an online market-research panel; stratified quota sampling with balanced quotas by region of the state for gender, age, race, education and ethnicity, benchmarked to US Census Bureau population estimates and Florida's Office of Economic and Demographic Research; stated margin of error +/-4 points at 95% confidence. Table 1 shows the achieved sample matching state demographics on most quotas but differing significantly on 18-24 year olds (7.8% vs 10.8%), White (73.5% vs 77.3%), Pacific Islander, Other race, and the West Coast and Southeast Florida regions. Responses were required for every question so there is no item missingness; multiple embedded quality-control questions, with failures excluded from the dataset. Exposure measured by eight named misinformation themes from a literature review plus CDC and other public-health guidance; principal-components factor analysis (varimax) found no theoretically distinct sub-categories. Analysis by descriptive statistics, chi-square with phi, and a logit model with robust standard errors (IBM SPSS v26; STATA v17). IRB exempt - a de-identified dataset purchased from the vendor, no human-subject contact by the authors. Author-acknowledged limitations: the web panel under-represents those without a high-school degree and rural residents lacking reliable internet, excludes under-18s and incarcerated residents and probably under-samples assisted-care residents; Florida-only; cross-sectional, so exposure and vaccination cannot be time-ordered; and the eight themes are an acknowledged proxy that misses other misinformation.
